claim: Osteogenic differentiation of skeletal progenitors is a key determinant of overall bone formation and bone mass.
source: Emerging evidence supports that osteogenic differentiation of skeletal progenitors is a key determinant of overall bone formation and bone mass.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general statement about the field, supported by emerging evidence.

claim: The ERK pathway in osteoblasts controls bone formation by suppressing the mTOR pathway.
source: Here, we describe how the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway in osteoblasts controls bone formation by suppressing the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: ERK inhibition blocks the differentiation of osteogenic precursors when initiated at an early stage.
source: We also show that, while ERK inhibition blocks the differentiation of osteogenic precursors when initiated at an early stage, ERK inhibition surprisingly promotes the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: ERK inhibition promotes the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
source: We also show that, while ERK inhibition blocks the differentiation of osteogenic precursors when initiated at an early stage, ERK inhibition surprisingly promotes the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1E-I.

claim: Inhibition of the ERK pathway using a small compound inhibitor or conditional deletion of MEK1 and MEK2 in mature osteoblasts and osteocytes markedly increased bone formation due to augmented osteoblast differentiation.
source: Accordingly, inhibition of the ERK pathway using a small compound inhibitor or conditional deletion of the MAP2Ks Map2k1 (MEK1) and Map2k2 (MEK2), in mature osteoblasts and osteocytes, markedly increased bone formation due to augmented osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Mice with inducible deletion of the ERK pathway in mature osteoblasts displayed increased bone formation phenotypes.
source: Mice with inducible deletion of the ERK pathway in mature osteoblasts also displayed similar phenotypes, demonstrating that this phenotype reflects continuous postnatal inhibition of late-stage osteoblast maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: ERK inhibition increases mitochondrial function via mTOR2 activation.
source: Mechanistically, ERK inhibition increases mitochondrial function and SGK1 phosphorylation via mTOR2 activation, which leads to osteoblast differentiation and production of angiogenic and osteogenic factors to promote bone formation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: ERK inhibition increases SGK1 phosphorylation via mTOR2 activation.
source: Mechanistically, ERK inhibition increases mitochondrial function and SGK1 phosphorylation via mTOR2 activation, which leads to osteoblast differentiation and production of angiogenic and osteogenic factors to promote bone formation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: The phenotype of increased bone formation in MEK1/2-deficient mice was partially reversed by inhibiting mTOR.
source: This phenotype was partially reversed by inhibiting mTOR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: ERK activation promotes the early differentiation of osteoblast precursors.
source: Our study uncovers a surprising dichotomy of ERK pathway functions in osteoblasts, whereby ERK activation promotes the early differentiation of osteoblast precursors, but inhibits the subsequent differentiation of committed osteoblasts via mTOR-mediated regulation of mitochondrial function and SGK1.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: ERK inhibits the subsequent differentiation of committed osteoblasts via mTOR-mediated regulation of mitochondrial function and SGK1.
source: Our study uncovers a surprising dichotomy of ERK pathway functions in osteoblasts, whereby ERK activation promotes the early differentiation of osteoblast precursors, but inhibits the subsequent differentiation of committed osteoblasts via mTOR-mediated regulation of mitochondrial function and SGK1.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Trametinib treatment prevented femoral bone loss in ovariectomized mice.
source: While OVX surgery induced a significant bone loss in the femur of vehicle-treated mice, femoral bone loss was prevented by treatment with trametinib, as shown by a greater trabecular bone volume (Tb. BV) and trabecular thickness (Tb. Th; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microCT data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Trametinib treatment increased bone formation rate per bone surface and osteoblast surface in ovariectomized mice.
source: Remarkably, dynamic histomorphometry analysis demonstrated an increase in bone formation rate per bone surface (BFR/BS) and osteoblast surface on the trabecular bone area (Ob.S/BS) of trametinib-treated OVX mice (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: ERK inhibition prevents estrogen deficiency-induced bone loss by promoting bone formation due to augmented osteoblast activity.
source: Thus, ERK inhibition prevents estrogen deficiency-induced bone loss by promoting bone formation due to augmented osteoblast activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OVX experiment data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Expression of RUNX2 and SP7 was markedly upregulated 8 days after osteogenic culture of human BMSCs.
source: Expression of key osteogenic commitment factors, RUNX2 and SP7 (Osterix), was markedly upregulated 8 days after osteogenic culture as expected, establishing that the BMSCs at this time point represent committed osteoblast-lineage cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERK inhibition starting at day 8 of culture promoted osteoblast differentiation of human BMSCs.
source: ERK inhibition starting at day 8 of culture promoted osteoblast differentiation, whereas ERK inhibition from day 0 of culture conversely inhibited proliferation and osteogenic potential of BMSCs (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ERK inhibition from day 0 of culture inhibited proliferation and osteogenic potential of human BMSCs.
source: ERK inhibition starting at day 8 of culture promoted osteoblast differentiation, whereas ERK inhibition from day 0 of culture conversely inhibited proliferation and osteogenic potential of BMSCs (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Trametinib treatment of mouse calvarial osteoblasts increased alkaline phosphatase activity, mineralization, and expression of osteogenic genes.
source: Similar findings were observed with committed osteoblasts isolated from mouse calvarium, which also showed increased osteogenic differentiation in the presence of trametinib. This was evident in ERK inhibitor induced increases in alkaline phosphatase (ALP), mineralization, and expression of osteogenic genes, including integrin-binding sialoprotein (Ibsp) and osteocalcin (Bglap; Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: Cell proliferation rates of mouse calvarial osteoblasts were largely unaffected by trametinib treatment.
source: Notably, cell proliferation rates were largely unaffected (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway plays a positive role in the early stages of osteogenesis.
source: These results suggest that while the ERK MAPK pathway plays a positive role in the early stages of osteogenesis, it acts as a negative regulator of the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway acts as a negative regulator of the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
source: These results suggest that while the ERK MAPK pathway plays a positive role in the early stages of osteogenesis, it acts as a negative regulator of the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of MEK1/2 in mature osteoblasts and osteocytes resulted in a significant increase in femoral bone mass.
source: Deletion of MEK1/2 was confirmed in RNA from the tibiae of WT and Map2k1fl/fl;Dmp1Cre;Map2k2−/− (double knockout, dKODmp1) mice (Figure 2A), and resulted in a significant increase in femoral bone mass, as evidenced by greater trabecular bone volume (Tb. BV), thickness (Tb. Th), number (Tb. N), and cortical thickness (Ct. Th; Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Skull thickness and L4 vertebrae trabecular bone volume were markedly increased in dKODmp1 mice.
source: Likewise, skull thickness and L4 vertebrae trabecular bone volume/tissue volume (Tb. BV/TV) were markedly increased (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Deletion of both MEK1 and MEK2 alleles is required for the increase in bone mass, as deletion of MEK1 or MEK2 alone did not show an increase in bone mass.
source: These skeletal phenotypes require the deletion of both MEK1 and MEK2 alleles as deletion of MEK1 (Map2k1 fl/fl;Dmp1Cre) or MEK2 (Map2k2−/−) alone did not show an increase in bone mass compared to WT femurs (Figure 2C), suggesting a redundant role for MEK1 and MEK2 in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MEK1 and MEK2 have a redundant role in osteoblasts.
source: These skeletal phenotypes require the deletion of both MEK1 and MEK2 alleles as deletion of MEK1 (Map2k1 fl/fl;Dmp1Cre) or MEK2 (Map2k2−/−) alone did not show an increase in bone mass compared to WT femurs (Figure 2C), suggesting a redundant role for MEK1 and MEK2 in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of both MEK1 and MEK2 is required for the phenotype.

claim: dKODmp1 femurs showed an increase in maximum bending moment and load at failure.
source: Consistent with the increased bone mass observed, a three-point bending test of dKODmp1 mice revealed an increase in maximum bending moment and load at failure, demonstrating enhanced bone mechanical strength (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The bone formed by ERK pathway ablation in late-stage osteoblasts has the biomechanical properties of mature, physiologic bone and not that of fracture-prone pathologic bone.
source: Thus, the bone formed by ERK pathway ablation in late-stage osteoblasts has the biomechanical properties of mature, physiologic bone and not that of fracture-prone pathologic bone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biomechanical testing data in Figure 2F.

claim: dKODmp1 femurs showed a significant increase in bone formation rate per bone surface and mineral apposition rate.
source: Finally, dynamic histomorphometry analysis demonstrated a significant increase in BFR/BS and mineral apposition rate (MAR) of dKODmp1 femurs, indicating enhanced in vivo osteoblast activity in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Deletion of MEK1/2 in late-stage osteoblast-lineage cells augmented their bone-forming activity and bone accrual and strength.
source: Therefore, deletion of MEK1/2 in late-stage osteoblast-lineage cells augmented their bone-forming activity and bone accrual and strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2B-G.

claim: In vivo osteoclast activity and numbers were markedly elevated in dKODmp1 mice.
source: Importantly, in vivo osteoclast activity and numbers were markedly elevated in dKODmp1 mice, as shown by an increase in tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP)-positive osteoclasts, bone erosion surface, and serum levels of the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide type I collagen (CTx-I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining and ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG) was reduced in dKODmp1 mice without any alteration in RANKL expression.
source: This was accompanied with reduced expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG, Tnfrsf11b) without any alteration in receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (RANKL, Tnfsf11) expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the upregulation of RANKL/OPG ratio may be responsible for the enhanced osteoclast activity observed in these mice.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The upregulation of RANKL/OPG ratio may be responsible for the enhanced osteoclast activity observed in dKODmp1 mice.
source: This was accompanied with reduced expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG, Tnfrsf11b) without any alteration in receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (RANKL, Tnfsf11) expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the upregulation of RANKL/OPG ratio may be responsible for the enhanced osteoclast activity observed in these mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced OPG expression and increased osteoclast activity.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment of dKOBglap mice significantly increased trabecular bone mass of the femur.
source: Treatment of mice with tamoxifen (dKOBglap) significantly increased trabecular bone mass of the femur (Figure 2H,I), demonstrating that the inhibitory role of the ERK MAPK pathway is specific to mature osteoblasts and reflects the continuous function of ERK in these cells and is not secondary to a developmental abnormality.
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: The inhibitory role of the ERK MAPK pathway is specific to mature osteoblasts and reflects the continuous function of ERK in these cells and is not secondary to a developmental abnormality.
source: Treatment of mice with tamoxifen (dKOBglap) significantly increased trabecular bone mass of the femur (Figure 2H,I), demonstrating that the inhibitory role of the ERK MAPK pathway is specific to mature osteoblasts and reflects the continuous function of ERK in these cells and is not secondary to a developmental abnormality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inducible knockout experiment shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: Osteocyte apoptosis was substantially increased in the cortical bone of dKODmp1 mice relative to control mice.
source: Osteocyte apoptosis was substantially increased in the cortical bone of dKODmp1 mice relative to control mice, which corresponded to decreased osteocyte numbers and increased empty lacunae (a cavity within the bone; Figure 2J, bottom, K).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining and histological analysis shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claim: Terminally differentiated osteocytes embedded in the bone matrix undergo apoptosis in dKODmp1 femurs.
source: Likewise, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of dKODmp1 femurs demonstrated that terminally differentiated osteocytes embedded in the bone matrix undergo apoptosis (Figure 2 L3) while osteocytes at early (Figure 2 L1) and intermediate (Figure 2 L2) differentiation stages were grossly normal in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: mRNA levels of early osteocyte markers Dmp1 and Phex were comparable between control and dKODmp1 tibias.
source: This is consistent with RT-PCR analysis showing that mRNA levels of early osteocyte markers, including dentin matrix protein1 (Dmp1) and phosphate regulating endopeptidase homolog X-linked (Phex) were comparable between control and dKODmp1 tibias.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of the late osteocyte marker sclerostin (Sost) was significantly decreased in dKODmp1 tibias.
source: However, expression of the late osteocyte marker, sclerostin (Sost), was significantly decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ERK activation is required for the survival of late/fully mature osteocytes, but not the transition of mature osteoblasts to early osteocytes.
source: These results suggest that ERK activation is required for the survival of late/fully mature osteocytes, but not the transition of mature osteoblasts to early osteocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early osteocyte markers are normal but late osteocytes undergo apoptosis in dKODmp1 mice.

claim: ERK inhibition in mature osteoblasts promotes bone formation, while impaired ERK signaling in late osteocytes results in cell death.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ERK inhibition in mature osteoblasts promotes bone formation, while impaired ERK signaling in late osteocytes results in cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2.

claim: Cre-induced deletion of MEK1 and MEK2 in committed osteoblasts increased ALP activity, mineralization, and osteogenic gene expression.
source: As seen in dKODmp1 mice, Cre-induced deletion of MEK1 and MEK2 MAP2Ks in committed osteoblasts increased ALP activity, mineralization, and osteogenic gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: Deletion of MEK1 or MEK2 alone did not impact osteogenic differentiation.
source: Deletion of MEK1 or MEK2 alone did not impact osteogenic differentiation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Proliferation rates of control osteoblasts were markedly increased under osteogenic conditions, but little to no increase was observed in the absence of MEK1/2.
source: While proliferation rates of control osteoblasts were markedly increased under osteogenic conditions, little to no increase was observed in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 3D), suggesting that ERK inhibition may control a shift toward differentiation at the expense of proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ERK inhibition may control a shift toward differentiation at the expense of proliferation.
source: While proliferation rates of control osteoblasts were markedly increased under osteogenic conditions, little to no increase was observed in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 3D), suggesting that ERK inhibition may control a shift toward differentiation at the expense of proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proliferation is reduced while differentiation is increased in dKO osteoblasts.

claim: Under cell growth conditions, upregulated genes in dKO osteoblasts were highly enriched in the pathways involved in ossification, skeletal system morphogenesis, and connective tissue development.
source: Gene ontology analysis demonstrated that, under cell growth conditions, upregulated genes were highly enriched in the pathways involved in ossification, skeletal system morphogenesis, and connective tissue development (Figure 3E), consistent with an increase in ALP activity and expression of osteogenic genes in undifferentiated dKO osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ERK inhibition induces spontaneous osteogenic differentiation by upregulating transcription of genes favorable to osteogenic differentiation.
source: These results suggest that ERK inhibition induces spontaneous osteogenic differentiation by upregulating transcription of genes favorable to osteogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene ontology analysis and expression data in undifferentiated dKO osteoblasts.

claim: Under osteogenic conditions, gene ontology analysis of differentiated dKO osteoblasts revealed upregulation of genes associated with extracellular matrix organization.
source: Under osteogenic conditions, gene ontology analysis of differentiated dKO osteoblasts revealed upregulation of genes associated with extracellular matrix organization, while genes related to cell proliferation, including nuclear division and cell cycle, were downregulated (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Under osteogenic conditions, genes related to cell proliferation, including nuclear division and cell cycle, were downregulated in dKO osteoblasts.
source: Under osteogenic conditions, gene ontology analysis of differentiated dKO osteoblasts revealed upregulation of genes associated with extracellular matrix organization, while genes related to cell proliferation, including nuclear division and cell cycle, were downregulated (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Impaired ERK signaling in later stage committed osteoblasts upregulates transcriptional programs associated with osteogenic differentiation while suppressing the induction of genes associated with cell proliferation.
source: These results suggest that impaired ERK signaling in later stage committed osteoblasts upregulates transcriptional programs associated with osteogenic differentiation while suppressing the induction of genes associated with cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptome analysis data in Figures 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes associated with the pro-osteogenic WNT/β-catenin and TGF-β signaling pathways were highly upregulated in dKO osteoblasts under osteogenic, but not undifferentiated, conditions.
source: Intriguingly, the genes associated with the pro-osteogenic WNT/β-catenin and TGF-β signaling pathways were highly upregulated in dKO osteoblasts under osteogenic, but not undifferentiated, conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA and gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Activities of β-catenin and Smads were significantly increased in dKO osteoblasts under osteogenic, but not undifferentiated, conditions.
source: This is consistent with luciferase assays showing a significant increase in activities of key transcription factors of WNT and TGF-β signaling, β-catenin and Smads, in the absence of MEK1/2 under osteogenic, but not undifferentiated, conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Protein levels of β-catenin and Smad3 in dKO cells cultured under osteogenic conditions were markedly increased.
source: Likewise, protein levels of β-catenin and Smad3 in dKO cells cultured under osteogenic conditions were markedly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that ERK inhibition at later stages of osteogenic differentiation enhances the pro-osteogenic WNT and TGF-β signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: ERK inhibition at later stages of osteogenic differentiation enhances the pro-osteogenic WNT and TGF-β signaling pathways.
source: Likewise, protein levels of β-catenin and Smad3 in dKO cells cultured under osteogenic conditions were markedly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that ERK inhibition at later stages of osteogenic differentiation enhances the pro-osteogenic WNT and TGF-β signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased protein levels and transcriptional activity of WNT and TGF-β pathway components.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of WNT and TGF-β signaling pathways reversed enhanced osteogenesis of dKO cells.
source: Accordingly, pharmacological inhibition of these signaling pathways reversed enhanced osteogenesis of dKO cells, as shown by reduced ALP activity and osteogenic gene expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C-F.

claim: Enhanced WNT and TGF-β signaling at later stages of osteogenic differentiation of dKO osteoblasts might be major contributors to drive osteogenic differentiation program.
source: These results suggest that enhanced WNT and TGF-β signaling at later stages of osteogenic differentiation of dKO osteoblasts might be major contributors to drive osteogenic differentiation program.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibiting these pathways reverses the enhanced osteogenesis in dKO cells.

claim: The expression and transcriptional activity of RUNX2 and SP7 were not strongly impacted in mature dKO osteoblasts.
source: While the expression and transcriptional activity of RUNX2 and SP7 were not strongly impacted in mature dKO osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C), ERK inhibition in mature osteoblasts markedly increased the expression and transcription activity of ATF4 (OSE1-luc; Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: ERK inhibition in mature osteoblasts markedly increased the expression and transcription activity of ATF4.
source: While the expression and transcriptional activity of RUNX2 and SP7 were not strongly impacted in mature dKO osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C), ERK inhibition in mature osteoblasts markedly increased the expression and transcription activity of ATF4 (OSE1-luc; Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, E.

claim: During the later stages of osteoblast differentiation, the ERK MAPK pathway is required for post-translational modifications of ATF4, but not RUNX2 and SP7.
source: These results suggest that during the later stages of osteoblast differentiation, the ERK MAPK pathway is required for post-translational modifications of ATF4, but not RUNX2 and SP7.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of ERK inhibition on RUNX2/SP7 versus ATF4.

claim: Whole transcriptome analysis of dKO osteoblasts revealed significant upregulation of secreted cytokines and/or growth factors involved in ossification and angiogenesis/vasculature development.
source: Whole transcriptome analysis of dKO osteoblasts also revealed significant upregulation of secreted cytokines and/or growth factors involved in ossification and angiogenesis/vasculature development (Figure 3F), such as fibroblast growth factor 9 (Fgf9; Behr et al., 2010), ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 2 (Enpp2; Cholia et al., 2015), transforming growth factor-beta 2 (Tgfb2; Wu et al., 2016), insulin-like growth factors 1, 2 (Igf1, 2; Yakar et al., 2018), bone morphogenic proteins 1, 3 (Bmp1, 3; Wu et al., 2016), C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 5 (Ccl5; Suffee et al., 2012), and Ccl11 (Salcedo et al., 2001; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figures 3F and 3G, with citations to prior literature.

claim: Conditioned medium collected from dKO osteoblasts markedly increased osteogenic potentials of wildtype BMSCs.
source: Accordingly, conditioned medium (CM), collected from dKO osteoblasts, markedly increased osteogenic potentials of wildtype BMSCs (Figure 3H) and capillary tube formation of bone marrow-derived endothelial progenitor outgrowth cells (EPOCs, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Conditioned medium collected from dKO osteoblasts markedly increased capillary tube formation of bone marrow-derived endothelial progenitor outgrowth cells (EPOCs).
source: Accordingly, conditioned medium (CM), collected from dKO osteoblasts, markedly increased osteogenic potentials of wildtype BMSCs (Figure 3H) and capillary tube formation of bone marrow-derived endothelial progenitor outgrowth cells (EPOCs, Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: dKODmp1 femurs showed elevated levels of CD31- and endomucin-positive skeletal vasculature.
source: Likewise, an immunofluorescence analysis of dKODmp1 femurs showed elevated levels of CD31- and endomucin-positive skeletal vasculature supporting osteoblast development (Xu et al., 2018; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3J, with citation to prior literature.

claim: Pro-angiogenic and/or -osteogenic factors secreted from dKO osteoblasts enhance angiogenesis and osteogenesis, promoting bone formation.
source: These results suggest that pro-angiogenic and/or -osteogenic factors secreted from dKO osteoblasts enhance angiogenesis and osteogenesis, promoting bone formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the conditioned medium experiments and immunofluorescence data.

claim: MEK1/2 deficiency increases osteoblast differentiation by upregulating osteogenic transcriptional programs and improves bone-forming environment by producing pro-angiogenic and/or -osteogenic factors.
source: Taken together, MEK1/2 deficiency does not only increase osteoblast differentiation by upregulating osteogenic transcriptional programs, but also improves bone-forming environment by producing pro-angiogenic and/or -osteogenic factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3.

claim: The differentiation of dKO osteoblasts was substantially reduced by glutaminase inhibition but only modestly impacted by glucose deprivation.
source: Remarkably, the differentiation of dKO osteoblasts was substantially reduced by glutaminase inhibition but only modestly impacted by glucose deprivation (Figure 4A, B), demonstrating the importance of glutamine metabolism in ERK-mediated regulation of osteogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Glutamine metabolism is important in ERK-mediated regulation of osteogenesis.
source: Remarkably, the differentiation of dKO osteoblasts was substantially reduced by glutaminase inhibition but only modestly impacted by glucose deprivation (Figure 4A, B), demonstrating the importance of glutamine metabolism in ERK-mediated regulation of osteogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of glutaminase inhibition versus glucose deprivation.

claim: The responsiveness of dKO osteoblasts to the glutaminase inhibitor BPTES was greater than that of control osteoblasts.
source: Specifically, the responsiveness of dKO osteoblasts to the glutaminase inhibitor (bis-2-[5-phenylacetamido-1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-yl]ethyl sulfide or BPTES) was greater than that of control osteoblasts, as shown by a significant reduction in ALP activity, cell proliferation, and osteogenic gene expression in the presence of BPTES (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: dKO osteoblasts showed elevated levels of glutaminase (Gls).
source: Likewise, these cells showed elevated levels of glutaminase (Gls), a key enzyme that produces glutamate from glutamine (Figure 4D), and increased glutamate production and release (Figure 4E), suggesting enhanced glutamine metabolism in dKO osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: dKO osteoblasts showed increased glutamate production and release.
source: Likewise, these cells showed elevated levels of glutaminase (Gls), a key enzyme that produces glutamate from glutamine (Figure 4D), and increased glutamate production and release (Figure 4E), suggesting enhanced glutamine metabolism in dKO osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by glutamate measurement data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: dKO osteoblasts have enhanced glutamine metabolism.
source: Likewise, these cells showed elevated levels of glutaminase (Gls), a key enzyme that produces glutamate from glutamine (Figure 4D), and increased glutamate production and release (Figure 4E), suggesting enhanced glutamine metabolism in dKO osteoblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased Gls expression and glutamate production.

claim: The effect of glucose deprivation on osteoblast maturation was intact in the absence of MEK1/2.
source: Of note, in contrast to previous studies showing critical roles of glucose metabolism (Wei et al., 2015), effect of glucose depravation on osteoblast maturation was intact in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 4A), suggesting that the ERK MAPK pathway is not required for glucose metabolism during the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, with citation to prior literature.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway is not required for glucose metabolism during the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
source: Of note, in contrast to previous studies showing critical roles of glucose metabolism (Wei et al., 2015), effect of glucose depravation on osteoblast maturation was intact in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 4A), suggesting that the ERK MAPK pathway is not required for glucose metabolism during the later stages of osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose deprivation has similar effects in control and dKO osteoblasts.

claim: dKO osteoblasts showed increased intracellular ATP levels.
source: Given the importance of glutamine metabolism in mitochondria-mediated energy production, we next examined the intracellular ATP content in dKO osteoblasts and found increased ATP levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials were markedly increased in dKO or trametinib-treated osteoblasts compared to control or vehicle-treated osteoblasts.
source: Additionally, mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials and a ratio of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) levels to nuclear DNA (nDNA) levels in dKO or trametinib-treated osteoblasts were all markedly increased compared to control or vehicle-treated osteoblasts (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and microscopy data shown in Figures 4G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) levels to nuclear DNA (nDNA) levels was markedly increased in dKO or trametinib-treated osteoblasts.
source: Additionally, mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials and a ratio of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) levels to nuclear DNA (nDNA) levels in dKO or trametinib-treated osteoblasts were all markedly increased compared to control or vehicle-treated osteoblasts (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: dKO osteoblasts showed enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR).
source: This corresponds to enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR), an indicator of cellular respiration, in dKO osteoblasts (Figure 4J), demonstrating that ERK inhibition promotes mitochondrial function and metabolic activity in committed osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by OCR measurement data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: ERK inhibition promotes mitochondrial function and metabolic activity in committed osteoblasts.
source: This corresponds to enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR), an indicator of cellular respiration, in dKO osteoblasts (Figure 4J), demonstrating that ERK inhibition promotes mitochondrial function and metabolic activity in committed osteoblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased mitochondrial numbers, membrane potential, and OCR in dKO osteoblasts.

claim: Levels of reactive oxidative species (ROS) were markedly elevated in dKO osteoblasts.
source: Finally, levels of reactive oxidative species (ROS; Figure 4K) and mRNA levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (Pgc1a), dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), and mitofusin 1 (Mfn1; Figure 4L), genes that are important for mitochondrial biogenesis, fission, and fusion, were also markedly elevated in dKO osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: mRNA levels of Pgc1a, Drp1, and Mfn1 were markedly elevated in dKO osteoblasts.
source: Finally, levels of reactive oxidative species (ROS; Figure 4K) and mRNA levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (Pgc1a), dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), and mitofusin 1 (Mfn1; Figure 4L), genes that are important for mitochondrial biogenesis, fission, and fusion, were also markedly elevated in dKO osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: ERK inhibition increases osteoblast differentiation via augmented glutamine metabolism and mitochondrial function.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ERK inhibition increases osteoblast differentiation via augmented glutamine metabolism and mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 4.

claim: Rapamycin treatment attenuated ALP activity and expression of osteogenic genes in dKO osteoblasts.
source: Rapamycin was used to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 activation (Lamming et al., 2012) in dKO osteoblasts, demonstrating that rapamycin treatment attenuated ALP activity (Figure 5B) and expression of osteogenic genes (Figure 5C) in the absence of MEK1/2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C, with citation to prior literature.

claim: Rapamycin treatment was effective at inhibiting the phosphorylation of the mTORC2 downstream molecules AKT and SGK1 in dKO osteoblasts.
source: Of note, in contrast to many contexts where rapamycin solely inhibits the mTORC1 pathway, including p70S6 kinase (p70S6K), rapamycin treatment was effective at inhibiting the phosphorylation of the mTORC2 downstream molecules, protein kinase B (AKT) and serum/glucocorticoid regulated kinase 1 (SGK1), in dKO osteoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rapamycin treatment decreases the differentiation of dKO osteoblasts by inhibiting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 pathways.
source: These results suggest that rapamycin treatment decreases the differentiation of dKO osteoblasts by inhibiting both mTORC1 and mTOCR2 pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rapamycin inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2 signaling and reduces osteogenic differentiation.

claim: Rapamycin treatment decreased trabecular bone mass and cortical bone thickness in dKODmp1 mice relative to vehicle.
source: While little effect of rapamycin on femoral bone mass was seen in control mice, trabecular bone mass and cortical bone thickness were both decreased in dKODmp1 mice when treated with rapamycin relative to vehicle, as shown by a significant reduction in trabecular bone volume (Tb. BV), number (Tb. N), thickness (Tb. Th), and cortical thickness (Ct.Th) (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: mTOR inhibition can reverse the enhanced bone-forming activity by MEK1/2-deletion in mice.
source: These results suggest, as observed in dKO osteoblasts, mTOR inhibition can reverse the enhanced bone-forming activity by MEK1/2-deletion in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rapamycin treatment reduces bone mass in dKODmp1 mice.

claim: mTOR inhibition was effective in preventing the osteocyte apoptosis occurring in the absence of MEK1/2.
source: A histologic analysis of rapamycin-treated dKODmp1 femurs revealed that mTOR inhibition was also effective in preventing the osteocyte apoptosis occurring in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Rapamycin treatment slightly decreased osteoclast surface in the trabecular bone of dKODmp1 femurs.
source: Additionally, osteoclast surface (Oc.S) in the trabecular bone was slightly decreased in these femurs, suggesting that rapamycin treatment may directly suppress osteoclast differentiation and activity (Glantschnig et al., 2003; Kneissel et al., 2004; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by TRAP staining data shown in Figure 5G, with citations to prior literature.

claim: Rapamycin treatment may directly suppress osteoclast differentiation and activity.
source: Additionally, osteoclast surface (Oc.S) in the trabecular bone was slightly decreased in these femurs, suggesting that rapamycin treatment may directly suppress osteoclast differentiation and activity (Glantschnig et al., 2003; Kneissel et al., 2004; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased osteoclast surface and cited literature.

claim: Impaired ERK signaling promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation via activation of the mTOR pathway.
source: Taken together, impaired ERK signaling is likely to promote osteogenic differentiation and bone formation via activation of the mTOR pathway, whose inhibition can reverse dKODmp1 phenotypes in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 5.

claim: dKO osteoblasts showed a significant increase in phosphorylation levels of mTORC2 downstream molecules, including AKT, SGK1, and NDRG1.
source: In comparison to control osteoblasts, dKO osteoblasts showed a significant increase in phosphorylation levels of mTORC2 downstream molecules, including AKT, SGK1, and NDRG1, whereas little to no alteration in the phosphorylation levels of the mTORC1 downstream molecules p70S6K and 4EBP1 were detected in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Little to no alteration in the phosphorylation levels of the mTORC1 downstream molecules p70S6K and 4EBP1 were detected in dKO osteoblasts.
source: In comparison to control osteoblasts, dKO osteoblasts showed a significant increase in phosphorylation levels of mTORC2 downstream molecules, including AKT, SGK1, and NDRG1, whereas little to no alteration in the phosphorylation levels of the mTORC1 downstream molecules p70S6K and 4EBP1 were detected in the absence of MEK1/2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ERK inhibition in osteoblasts activates mTORC2- but not mTORC1-mediated signal transduction.
source: Together with previous studies (Brown et al., 2020; Umapathy et al., 2017), these results suggest that ERK inhibition in osteoblasts activates mTORC2- but not mTORC1-mediated signal transduction via phosphorylation of mTORC2 subunits, Rictor or SIN1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential phosphorylation of mTORC2 versus mTORC1 substrates, with citations to prior literature.

claim: Sgk1 knockdown markedly attenuated ALP activity, expression of osteogenic genes, and mineralization in dKO osteoblasts, not in control osteoblasts.
source: Similar to rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition (Figure 5B, C), Sgk1 knockdown markedly attenuated ALP activity (Figure 6B), expression of osteogenic genes (Figure 6C), and mineralization (Figure 6D) in dKO osteoblasts, not in control osteoblasts, suggesting that SGK1 functions downstream of ERK during osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: SGK1 functions downstream of ERK during osteoblast differentiation.
source: Similar to rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition (Figure 5B, C), Sgk1 knockdown markedly attenuated ALP activity (Figure 6B), expression of osteogenic genes (Figure 6C), and mineralization (Figure 6D) in dKO osteoblasts, not in control osteoblasts, suggesting that SGK1 functions downstream of ERK during osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sgk1 knockdown reverses the enhanced osteogenesis in dKO osteoblasts.

claim: The enhanced expression and transcription activity of ATF4 in mature dKO osteoblasts were reversed by Sgk1 knockdown or mitochondrial inhibitor treatment.
source: Notably, the enhanced expression and transcription activity of ATF4 in mature dKO osteoblasts were reversed by Sgk1 knockdown or mitochondrial inhibitor treatment, suggesting that mTOR–SGK1 and mitochondrial function control ERK-mediated regulation of ATF4 in mature osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, E.

claim: mTOR–SGK1 and mitochondrial function control ERK-mediated regulation of ATF4 in mature osteoblasts.
source: Notably, the enhanced expression and transcription activity of ATF4 in mature dKO osteoblasts were reversed by Sgk1 knockdown or mitochondrial inhibitor treatment, suggesting that mTOR–SGK1 and mitochondrial function control ERK-mediated regulation of ATF4 in mature osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sgk1 knockdown or mitochondrial inhibition reverses ATF4 upregulation.

claim: The ability of conditioned medium collected from dKO osteoblasts to promote angiogenesis of EPOCs and osteogenesis of wildtype BMSCs was ablated by Sgk1 knockdown.
source: Additionally, the ability of CM collected from dKO osteoblasts to promote angiogenesis of EPOCs and osteogenesis of wildtype BMSCs was ablated by Sgk1 knockdown, as shown by a significant decrease in migration of EPOCs (Figure 6E), and ALP activity and Col1a1 mRNA levels of BMSCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: Little to no alteration of mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials was observed in trametinib-treated Sgk1-deficient osteoblasts or Sgk1-deficient dKO osteoblasts.
source: Notably, little to no alteration of mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials (Figure 6G) and OCR (Figure 6H) was observed in trametinib-treated Sgk1-deficient osteoblasts or Sgk1-deficient dKO osteoblasts, suggesting that SGK1 is dispensable for ERK-mediated mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Little to no alteration of OCR was observed in trametinib-treated Sgk1-deficient osteoblasts or Sgk1-deficient dKO osteoblasts.
source: Notably, little to no alteration of mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials (Figure 6G) and OCR (Figure 6H) was observed in trametinib-treated Sgk1-deficient osteoblasts or Sgk1-deficient dKO osteoblasts, suggesting that SGK1 is dispensable for ERK-mediated mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is supported by OCR measurement data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: SGK1 is dispensable for ERK-mediated mitochondrial function.
source: Notably, little to no alteration of mitochondrial numbers and membrane potentials (Figure 6G) and OCR (Figure 6H) was observed in trametinib-treated Sgk1-deficient osteoblasts or Sgk1-deficient dKO osteoblasts, suggesting that SGK1 is dispensable for ERK-mediated mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sgk1 knockdown does not affect mitochondrial function.

claim: The ERK–mTORC2 signaling axis mediates osteogenesis and production of pro-angio/osteogenic factors via SGK1 activation.
source: Taken together, the ERK–mTORC2 signaling axis mediates osteogenesis and production of pro-angio/osteogenic factors via SGK1 activation, while controlling osteogenesis via mitochondria-dependent energy metabolism (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6, with a summary diagram in Figure 6I.

claim: The ERK–mTORC2 signaling axis controls osteogenesis via mitochondria-dependent energy metabolism.
source: Taken together, the ERK–mTORC2 signaling axis mediates osteogenesis and production of pro-angio/osteogenic factors via SGK1 activation, while controlling osteogenesis via mitochondria-dependent energy metabolism (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6, with a summary diagram in Figure 6I.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway transduces activation signals from extracellular cues, such as bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) and wingless-related integration site (WNT) ligands, determining the specification of skeletal progenitors to osteoprogenitors.
source: The extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) MAPK pathway transduces activation signals from extracellular cues, such as bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) and wingless-related integration site (WNT) ligands, determining the specification of skeletal progenitors to osteoprogenitors (Ge et al., 2007; Greenblatt et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2019; Matsushita et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Conditional deletion of Mapk1 (ERK2) and Mapk2 (ERK1) in the mesenchyme (Prrx1Cre) causes severe limb deformity and bone defects due to impaired osteogenesis.
source: For example, conditional deletion of Mapk1 (ERK2) and Mapk2 (ERK1) in the mesenchyme (Prrx1Cre) causes severe limb deformity and bone defects due to impaired osteogenesis (Matsushita et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice lacking MAP2K1 (MEK1) and MAP2K2 (MEK2) in osteoprogenitors (Sp7Cre) showed low bone mass and a cleidocranial dysplasia-like phenotype.
source: Similarly, mice lacking the MAP2Ks in the ERK pathway, Map2k1 (MAP2K1, MEK1) and Map2k2 (MAP2K2, MEK2), in osteoprogenitors (Sp7Cre) showed low bone mass and a cleidocranial dysplasia-like phenotype (CCD), similar to that seen in mice and humans with runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) haploinsufficiency (Ge et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: ERK-mediated activation of RUNX2 is required for the commitment of skeletal progenitors to osteoprogenitors and the subsequent proliferation of osteoprogenitors at early differentiation stages.
source: Thus, ERK-mediated activation of RUNX2 is required for the commitment of skeletal progenitors to osteoprogenitors and the subsequent proliferation of osteoprogenitors at early differentiation stages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from cited literature.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway mediates phosphorylation of ribosomal s6 kinase 2 (RSK2).
source: Additionally, the ERK MAPK pathway mediates phosphorylation of ribosomal s6 kinase 2 (RSK2; Yang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Rsk2-deficient mice and humans are osteopenic due to impaired production of type I collagen.
source: Rsk2-deficient mice and humans are osteopenic due to impaired production of type I collagen, the major organic component of bone.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: RSK2 mutations have been reported to be associated with Coffin–Lowry syndrome showing prominent skeletal dysplasia features.
source: RSK2 mutations have been reported to be associated with Coffin–Lowry syndrome showing prominent skeletal dysplasia features (David et al., 2005; Hanauer and Young, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of function mutations in NF1 cause neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) syndrome, characterized by a complex set of bone phenotypes that can include osteopenia and impaired fracture healing as well as cutaneous neurofibromas.
source: As neurofibromin 1 (NF1) functions as a negative regulator of the ERK MAPK pathway, loss of function mutations in NF1 cause neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) syndrome, characterized by a complex set of bone phenotypes that can include osteopenia and impaired fracture healing as well as cutaneous neurofibromas (Bok et al., 2020; Crawford and Schorry, 1999; de la Croix Ndong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Gain of function mutations in PTPN11 (SHP2) enhance ERK signaling in osteoblasts, causing Noonan syndrome associated with impaired skeletal mineralization and short stature.
source: Similar to NF1, gain of function mutations in protein-tyrosine phosphatase nonreceptor-type 11 (PTPN11, SHP2) enhance ERK signaling in osteoblasts, causing Noonan syndrome associated with impaired skeletal mineralization and short stature (Binder, 2009; Choudhry et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: The ERK MAPK pathway controls the mTOR pathway, a signaling modulator of mitochondrial biogenesis that regulates cellular energy metabolism.
source: In addition to RUNX2, the ERK MAPK pathway controls the mTOR pathway, a signaling modulator of mitochondrial biogenesis that regulates cellular energy metabolism (Morita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: Cross-regulation between the ERK and mTOR pathways in various cancer cells has been reported.
source: Cross-regulation between these pathways in various cancer cells has been also reported (Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior literature.

claim: ERK inhibition by an MEK inhibitor activates the mTORC2–AKT signaling axis downstream of epidermal growth factor (EGF).
source: ERK inhibition by an MEK inhibitor activates the mTORC2–AKT signaling axis downstream of epidermal growth factor (EGF; Yu et al., 2002), and a similar increase in AKT activation by ERK inhibition was reported in anaplastic lymphoma kinase-addicted neuroblastoma (Umapathy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: Impaired ERK activation by the MEK inhibitor trametinib treatment enhanced phosphorylation of the mTORC2 complex subunits, Rictor or SIN1, via activation of induced integrin-linked kinase, resulting in AKT activation.
source: Mechanistically, impaired ERK activation by the MEK inhibitor trametinib treatment enhanced phosphorylation of the mTORC2 complex subunits, Rictor or stress-activated protein kinase (SAPK)-interacting protein 1 (SIN1), via activation of induced integrin-linked kinase, resulting in AKT activation (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Umapathy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: The ERK pathway is the most frequently mutated pathway in cancer.
source: Thus, determining the function and the regulatory mechanism of ERK in osteoblast differentiation and bone formation is clinically significant as the ERK pathway is the most frequently mutated pathway in cancer and, accordingly, ERK pathway components, including rat sarcoma (RAS), rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma, and MEK isoforms, are all well-established targets to treat a wide variety of ERK pathway-activated cancers (Hong et al., 2020; Hyman et al., 2015; Robert et al., 2015; Tiacci et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: ERK pathway components, including RAS, rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma, and MEK isoforms, are all well-established targets to treat a wide variety of ERK pathway-activated cancers.
source: Thus, determining the function and the regulatory mechanism of ERK in osteoblast differentiation and bone formation is clinically significant as the ERK pathway is the most frequently mutated pathway in cancer and, accordingly, ERK pathway components, including rat sarcoma (RAS), rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma, and MEK isoforms, are all well-established targets to treat a wide variety of ERK pathway-activated cancers (Hong et al., 2020; Hyman et al., 2015; Robert et al., 2015; Tiacci et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior literature.

claim: mTORC2 activation not only mediates osteogenesis and skeletal mineralization in response to growth factors or mechanical loading, but it also plays a role in the restoration of metabolic homeostasis in response to nutrient fluctuations.
source: On the other hand, mTORC2 activation not only mediates osteogenesis and skeletal mineralization in response to growth factors or mechanical loading, but it also plays a role in the restoration of metabolic homeostasis in response to nutrient fluctuations (Szwed et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: mTORC2 has been reported to be associated with age-related osteoporosis since impaired mTORC2 activation in aged mice switches the fate of skeletal progenitors to adipocytes from osteoblasts.
source: Additionally, mTORC2 has been reported to be associated with age-related osteoporosis since impaired mTORC2 activation in aged mice switches the fate of skeletal progenitors to adipocytes from osteoblasts (Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: mTORC2 activation is required for mitochondrial function and homeostasis.
source: This corresponds to previous reports showing that mTORC2 activation is required for mitochondrial function and homeostasis (Wang et al., 2021) and that both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by mitochondria are required to meet the energy demands needed for bone formation by osteoblasts (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: Both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by mitochondria are required to meet the energy demands needed for bone formation by osteoblasts.
source: This corresponds to previous reports showing that mTORC2 activation is required for mitochondrial function and homeostasis (Wang et al., 2021) and that both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by mitochondria are required to meet the energy demands needed for bone formation by osteoblasts (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: SGK1 played an important role in osteogenic trans-differentiation and calcification of vascular muscle cells.
source: In a previous study, SGK1, that functions downstream of mTORC2, played an important role in osteogenic trans-differentiation and calcification of vascular muscle cells (Voelkl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: Osteogenic precursors not only consume glutamine to generate ATP but also synthesize metabolites to promote osteoblast viability and matrix mineralization.
source: Previous studies have shown that osteogenic precursors not only consume glutamine to generate ATP but also synthesize metabolites to promote osteoblast viability and matrix mineralization (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: Systemic administration of rapamycin increases bone anabolic activity in both normal bone mass and osteopenic conditions.
source: Since systemic administration of rapamycin increases bone anabolic activity in both normal bone mass and osteopenic conditions (Bateman et al., 2019; Chagin, 2016; Izawa et al., 2017), rapamycin-induced attenuation of osteogenic differentiation and bone anabolic activity in MEK1/2-deficient mice and osteoblasts is unlikely to result from nonspecific or general effects of rapamycin unrelated to the specific defects in MEK1/2-deficient mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.
